name: Eyewitness memory
statement: Eyewitness memory is a field label rather than one effect, and its most argued recent finding is that confidence at a first, uncontaminated identification predicts accuracy well.
meaning: The label covers every way a witness's account of a crime can go wrong, and it is not one effect. Wells split the field in two in 1978 and the split still organises it. System variables are conditions the police control, such as who stands in the lineup, who administers it and what the witness is told first. Estimator variables are conditions nobody controls, such as lighting, viewing distance, delay and the race of the person seen. The outcome measures differ as well. A witness may fail to describe a face, fail to pick the right man from a lineup, pick an innocent one, or import a detail from a conversation or a newspaper. Those are separate failures with separate literatures, and this page is a map of the members that have their own entries here, because that is the level at which the evidence exists. Their verdicts do not agree, so an average over them would describe nothing. Weapon focus is unsettled at entry 160. The cross-race effect held at entry 78, memory conformity at entry 249, misattribution of memory at entry 239 and the misinformation effect at entry 502. False memory and suggestibility both came out mixed, at entries 35 and 172. The effect sizes behind those verdicts sit on those pages and were not re-read for this entry. What the umbrella has of its own is field data on real lineups, an archive of wrongful convictions, and one contested claim about the first memory test.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: 'Applied eyewitness-testimony research: System variables and estimator variables' gave the field the vocabulary it still uses. Its metadata was verified at Crossref and its text was not read for this entry. Wells and his co-authors cite it in the 2020 review, which was read, for both terms: system variables are conditions the justice system controls, estimator variables are conditions it does not. They add that the definition of a system variable has since broadened, from factors that influence accuracy to factors that merely relate to it, which is how eyewitness confidence came to be treated as one. No single publication founds the subject. Its policy spine is the 1998 review by Wells, Small, Penrod, Malpass, Fulero and Brimacombe, which the American Psychology-Law Society had updated by Wells, Kovera, Douglass, Brewer, Meissner and Wixted in 2020.

evidence: Real lineups produce errors that can be counted without knowing who is guilty, because a filler is known to be innocent. The 2020 review pools 11 peer-reviewed field studies covering 6,734 lineups from jurisdictions including California, Arizona, Texas and London. Across them 40.8% of witnesses identified the suspect, 23.7% identified a known-innocent filler and 35.5% identified nobody. Among the witnesses who picked someone, 36.8% picked a filler. The review sets that beside Clark, Howell and Davey's summary of 94 laboratory studies, where filler identifications averaged 21.2% with the culprit present and 34.6% with the culprit absent. It concludes that laboratory work does not inflate the rate of mistaken identification. The archive of wrongful convictions is the other umbrella-level record. Berkowitz, Garrett, Fenn and Loftus report that of the first 250 DNA exonerations in the United States, mistaken eyewitness identification occurred in 190, or 76%, a share inflated by DNA testing being most useful in stranger sexual assault cases. Trial records were obtained for 161 of those 190, or 85%. In 64 of the 161, or 40%, the witness had identified a filler, another suspect or nobody at the identification procedure. In 15, or 9%, the witness said they never saw the face. In 34, or 21%, the witness testified to having been uncertain at the time. Ninety-one of the 161, or 57%, carried at least one of those problems. The entire identification procedure was recorded in four of the 161. The same authors report 703 eyewitness exonerations among more than 2,400 in the National Registry of Exonerations as of July 2019. Eyewitness memory was the commonest route by which the exoneree first became a suspect, in 321 cases or 46%, a count they take from Kenchel, Loftus and Berkowitz. The confidence claim rests on a field study and a laboratory study built to be compared. Wixted, Mickes, Dunn, Clark and Wells worked with the Houston Police Department robbery division on photo lineups run between 22 January and 5 December 2013, with confidence recorded on a three-point scale. Their analysis covered 717 photo spreads that met the inclusion criteria, of which 348 were administered blind, yielding 114 suspect identifications, 104 filler identifications and 130 rejections. Fitting an equal variance signal detection model with the base rate free put the proportion of lineups containing a guilty suspect at 0.35, so 65% held an innocent suspect. A separate worked example in their supplement, which instead assumes equal base rates, starts from 71 high-confidence suspect identifications and 17 high-confidence filler identifications and estimates 68.9 correct against 2.1 incorrect suspect identifications, an accuracy of 0.97. The paper keeps those two fits apart, and it is Wixted and Mickes in 2025 who describe the Houston result as high-confidence accuracy approaching 97% correct. Ayala, Smith and Wells then ran a laboratory study of 6,230 people sharing the field study's features: both lineup formats, description-matched fillers, may-or-may-not-be-present instructions, five simulated viewing distances and an immediate confidence rating on a 100-point scale. Wixted and Mickes recomputed suspect identification accuracy directly from those data, which is possible in a laboratory because guilt is known, and got high-confidence accuracy of about 97% again. The same fit recovered known base rates of 0.50 and 0.61 as 0.45 and 0.60. The claim has also been tested by authors outside that group. Sauerland, Tupper, Iannuzzi and van Amelsvoort ran it under Dutch lineup protocols, under which three earlier Dutch experiments had found no confidence-accuracy association. They recruited 311 participants and analysed 293 after exclusions. The correlation was .41 for the 71 witnesses who picked someone, p < .001, and .19 for the 222 who did not, p = .004. The Houston conditions were not favourable ones: every crime was a robbery, a weapon was present in most cases, and most identifications were cross-race.

replication.headline: No replication attempt of eyewitness memory as a whole was located, because the label names a subject and not a procedure. The one field-level claim that has been repeated is the confidence claim, and it held in the Houston lineups, in the laboratory study built to mirror them, and in an independent Dutch test.
replication.detail: The state is a claim about the label, not about the field. What the search looked for and did not find is a repetition of eyewitness memory itself, and nothing carries that name, so there is no protocol to run again. The search ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall and general web search, for multi-laboratory, many-labs and registered-report work on eyewitness identification, and for repeats by the authors of the papers cited here. It returned a 2021 commentary by Lindsay and Mah arguing that eyewitness identification could be studied in multi-lab collaborations, which is an argument for such work rather than its result. The members were tested apart and their verdicts do not agree, so an average over them would describe nothing. Weapon focus is unsettled, with three meta-analyses reporting an effect on descriptions of the perpetrator, Steblay and Fawcett reporting a small effect on identification where Kocab and Sporer report none, and five preregistered experiments in one paper producing one marginal result and nothing else; entry 160. The cross-race effect held in a meta-analysis of 159 articles; entry 78. Memory conformity held in a ten-country replication; entry 249. Misattribution of memory held; entry 239. The misinformation effect held; entry 502. False memory and suggestibility both came out mixed; entries 35 and 172. The effect sizes behind those verdicts sit on those pages and were not re-read for this entry. The confidence claim is the one place where repetition can be judged here. Sauerland, Tupper, Iannuzzi and van Amelsvoort tested it under Dutch lineup protocols, which three earlier Dutch experiments had found no confidence-accuracy association under. They recruited 311 participants and analysed 293 after exclusions, and got a correlation of .41 for the 71 witnesses who picked someone, p < .001, against .19 for the 222 who did not, p = .004. Quigley-McBride and Wells took a different route to the same question, rating recorded confidence and decision time in real lineups, and report in their abstract that both predicted whether the witness picked the suspect or a known-innocent filler. Their full text was not obtained and no figure from it appears here. What the field itself thinks was measured once. Seale-Carlisle, Quigley-McBride, Teitcher, Crozier, Dodson and Garrett surveyed 76 eyewitness scientists between December 2020 and June 2021. Agreement ran to 100% on the wording of questions, on post-event information and on unconscious transference, 99% on blind lineups, 97% on cross-race bias, 93% on the forgetting curve, 89% on unfair lineups, 88% on showups and 80% on weapon focus. It fell to 68% on face recognition ability, 53% on low filler similarity and 28% on lineup rejections. Only 26 of the 76, or 34%, agreed that people are more accurate with sequential than with simultaneous lineups. The two confidence statements split by 21 points. Sixty-eight percent agreed that confidence stated in court, or at any time after the identification procedure, is a poor indicator of accuracy. Eighty-nine percent agreed that where best practices are used, confidence taken immediately after the decision can inform accuracy. The authors read that gap as a sensitivity to when confidence is collected rather than as disagreement, and trace the older position to the point-biserial correlation, which was often low. The confidence claim has drawn direct challenge on the estimator-variable side. Wixted and Mickes describe Giacona, Lampinen and Anastasi as having reanalysed the Houston cases. They sorted them by how many of seven estimator variables were suboptimal. Among high-confidence identifications, the proportion landing on the suspect rather than a filler fell from about 0.87 with a good view to 0.71 with a poor one. Giacona's own abstract describes something else, a laboratory experiment on 2,191 students, and does not mention the Houston data, so the provenance of those two figures could not be settled without the paper. Wixted and Mickes answer that the measure is not the one a court needs, and that computed directly in the Ayala data the equivalent good-view and poor-view figures are 98% and 96% correct, z = 1.08, p = 0.274. They also report, from Ayala's five simulated viewing distances, that the number of high-confidence suspect identifications fell from over 400 at 10 feet to 33 at 210 feet. Under 3% of participants made one at the longest distance, against 33% at the shortest. Their reading is that witnesses raise the bar for confidence as conditions worsen. Lockamyeir, Carlson, Jones, Carlson and Weatherford are the case that resists it. Their abstract reports high confidence tracking accuracy at 3 metres and 10 metres but not at 20 metres. As Wixted and Mickes describe that condition, 19 high-confidence suspect identifications were made by 1.6% of 1,194 participants, and were 63% correct.

limits: No meta-analysis, multi-site replication or registered report of eyewitness memory as a whole was located, and none could exist, because the label names a subject rather than a procedure. The search ran on 21 September 2026 across Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed Central, PubMed, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, the National Academies Press reader and general web search. Four documents could not be obtained, and in each case the block was a bot challenge rather than a paywall. Wells's 1978 paper is closed at the publisher, and APA's PsycNet and ResearchGate both answered with bot challenges. Only its Crossref record was read, and nothing about its argument is claimed here beyond what Wells and his co-authors attribute to it in 2020. Ayala, Smith and Wells is recorded as free at the publisher by both Unpaywall and OpenAlex, and the same PsycNet challenge blocked it. Its design details and every figure attributed to it are Wixted and Mickes's reanalysis of its data. Giacona, Lampinen and Anastasi is closed at the publisher; its abstract was read at Semantic Scholar and the 0.87 and 0.71 figures are quoted from Wixted and Mickes. Lockamyeir and colleagues is free to read at Wiley, which answered with a Cloudflare challenge; its abstract was read at Semantic Scholar and Moore and colleagues describe the same result independently. Sporer, Penrod, Read and Cutler's 1995 meta-analysis could not be reached at Crossref, Semantic Scholar, PsycNet or ResearchGate, and its coefficients are quoted here only through Wixted and Wells, who report .41 for choosers. Two claims the previous version of this page made about unobtainability were wrong and have been withdrawn. The 2016 field study's full text is on PubMed Central and was read there, and the 2020 policy review is a free PDF on the publisher's own site, so neither is quoted at one remove any longer. Wixted and Wells's 2017 synthesis was read as the accepted manuscript posted by its first author, not as the typeset journal version, and the two were not compared. Giacona's and Lockamyeir's figures are quoted from Wixted and Mickes's account of them, and Wixted and Mickes are parties to the dispute they are describing. The Houston estimates are model output, not counts. The 0.35 base rate and the 0.97 accuracy come from two different fits of an equal variance signal detection model to 348 lineups from one department in one year, and their validity rests on the model's assumptions. Wixted and Mickes report that allowing for suspect bias did not change the fit, which is evidence against one objection rather than against all of them. The Ayala study was run online with simulated viewing distances. Whether high-confidence accuracy survives conditions degraded further than those tested is described by Wixted and Mickes themselves as unresolved.
misreadings: The blanket reading is the commonest one. Eyewitness memory is treated as reliable or unreliable as a whole, when the unit that fails is a particular witness identifying a particular stranger under conditions that can be listed. The expert survey shows the field does not answer at one level either: agreement ran from 100% on post-event information to 28% on lineup rejections. The second error merges two moments. Courtroom confidence and confidence at the first test are different measurements, and the experts split 68% against 89% on them. The National Research Council's 2014 report makes the same distinction from the legal side, faulting the Manson v. Brathwaite test for treating witness confidence as an independent marker of reliability when confidence judgments vary over time and can be swayed by many factors, and recommending that police document confidence verbatim at the moment of first identification. Nothing in the recent work rehabilitates the certain witness on the stand. The third error drops the conditions. The 97% figure describes an initial, uncontaminated test using a fair lineup with one suspect, a blind administrator, a warning that the culprit may be absent and an immediate confidence statement. Moore, Pennekamp, Yu and Zwemer note that only 29 of the 50 states and the federal government have adopted any of those practices. They also report that 41% of one sample of real police lineups was biased against the suspect. Both figures are quoted in their review from Kafadar and colleagues and from Steblay and Wells. They also list the estimator variables under which high confidence has failed to track accuracy, including a three-day delay, poor face recognition ability, slow decisions, and witnesses aged four to nine. The fourth error runs the DNA figure backwards. Mistaken identification in 76% of the first 250 exonerations is a share of a set selected for having testable biological evidence, and it is not the rate at which witnesses are wrong. The fifth is a claim about those cases that the record cannot support. Berkowitz and colleagues show that no reliable measure of the exonerees' initial confidence exists, because the whole procedure was recorded in four of 161 cases and what survives is retrospective testimony at trial. Assertions that no such witness was both mistaken and highly confident go beyond what Garrett's data can settle. The sixth is about the meta-analysis the pessimistic reading is usually hung on. Sporer, Penrod, Read and Cutler are cited across the literature for a weak confidence-accuracy relation, and Wixted and Wells argue that what they reported was .41 among witnesses who picked someone, which is between a medium and a large effect. That figure is quoted here at second hand from a paper that is a party to the argument, and it does not go in the structured fields. The half of the claim nobody disputes is the low-confidence half. Wixted and Wells wrote that whereas the information value of a high-confidence identification may be called into question whenever non-pristine testing conditions are used, the information value of a low-confidence identification is never open to question. Berkowitz and colleagues, who dispute nearly everything else in that paper, say they do not disagree with it.

sources.text: Wells, G. L. (1978). Applied eyewitness-testimony research: System variables and estimator variables. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 36(12), 1546-1557. Not read. Closed at the publisher, and retried on 21 September 2026 at APA PsycNet and at ResearchGate, both of which answered with a bot challenge rather than a paywall. Only the Crossref record was read, and no claim about the paper's contents is made here except the one Wells and his co-authors attribute to it in the 2020 review.

Wixted, J. T., & Wells, G. L. (2017). The relationship between eyewitness confidence and identification accuracy: A new synthesis. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 18(1), 10-65. Read in full as the 136-page accepted manuscript posted by the first author at wixtedlab.ucsd.edu, not as the typeset journal version, which is closed. Source for the pristine-conditions argument, for the quotation about low-confidence identifications, and for the .41 that Sporer and colleagues report for choosers.

Wixted, J. T., Mickes, L., Dunn, J. C., Clark, S. E., & Wells, W. (2016). Estimating the reliability of eyewitness identifications from police lineups. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 113(2), 304-309. Read in full at PubMed Central, twice, and the two renderings were identical; a third request to the same address returned a reCAPTCHA challenge instead. Source for the 717 photo spreads, the 348 blind lineups and their outcomes, the 0.35 base rate and the supplement's 0.97 worked example.

Wixted, J. T., & Mickes, L. (2025). Suspect identification accuracy from lineups, in the lab and in the field. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 10, 48. Open access, read in full from the Europe PMC XML. Source for the Houston counts, the 35% base rate, the near-97% high-confidence accuracy, the comparison with Ayala and colleagues, and the descriptions of Giacona and of Lockamyeir.

Ayala, N. T., Smith, A. M., & Wells, G. L. (2025). Beyond the confidence-accuracy relation: A multiple-reflector-variable approach to postdicting accuracy on eyewitness lineups. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 31(3), 204-227. Not read. Unpaywall and OpenAlex both record the published version as free at the publisher, and APA PsycNet answered with a bot challenge on 21 September 2026. Metadata verified at Crossref and the abstract read at Semantic Scholar; the design details and all figures attributed to it here are Wixted and Mickes's (2025) reanalysis of its data.

Berkowitz, S. R., Garrett, B. L., Fenn, K. M., & Loftus, E. F. (2022). Convicting with confidence? Why we should not over-rely on eyewitness confidence. Memory, 30(1), 10-15. Read in full as the author's copy at eScholarship. Source for the DNA exoneration counts, the National Registry of Exonerations figures and the quotation from Wixted and Wells about low-confidence identifications.

Moore, K. N., Pennekamp, P., Yu, C., & Zwemer, D. U. (2024). Eyewitness confidence does not necessarily indicate identification accuracy. Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 11(2), 149-155. Read in full. Source for the adoption figures, the 41% biased-lineup figure and the list of estimator variables under which high confidence failed; those figures are its own quotations of Kafadar and colleagues, of Steblay and Wells, and of the individual studies.

Seale-Carlisle, T. M., Quigley-McBride, A., Teitcher, J. E. F., Crozier, W. E., Dodson, C. S., & Garrett, B. L. (2025). New insights on expert opinion about eyewitness memory research. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 20(5), 903-924. Read in full at Europe PMC. Source for the survey of 76 scientists and for every agreement percentage quoted here, including the 68% and 89% confidence statements, which were read twice.

Giacona, A. M., Lampinen, J. M., & Anastasi, J. S. (2021). Estimator variables can matter even for high-confidence lineup identifications made under pristine conditions. Law and Human Behavior, 45(3), 256-270. Not read; closed at the publisher and blocked by a bot challenge at PsycNet on 21 September 2026. Its abstract was read at Semantic Scholar and describes a laboratory experiment on 2,191 students; the Houston reanalysis and the 0.87 and 0.71 figures are Wixted and Mickes's (2025) account of the paper.

Lockamyeir, R. F., Carlson, C. A., Jones, A. R., Carlson, M. A., & Weatherford, D. R. (2020). The effect of viewing distance on empirical discriminability and the confidence-accuracy relationship for eyewitness identification. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 34(5), 1047-1060. Not read. Semantic Scholar records it as free to read at Wiley, which answered with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, so this is a bot block and not a paywall. Its abstract was read at Semantic Scholar and is the source for the 3, 10 and 20 metre result; the counts in the 20-metre condition are quoted from Wixted and Mickes (2025).

Wells, G. L., Kovera, M. B., Douglass, A. B., Brewer, N., Meissner, C. A., & Wixted, J. T. (2020). Policy and procedure recommendations for the collection and preservation of eyewitness identification evidence. Law and Human Behavior, 44(1), 3-36. Read in full as the free 34-page PDF the publisher posts at apa.org/pubs/journals/releases, downloaded twice to the same checksum. Source for the 11 field studies, the 6,734 lineups and every percentage in Table 1, and for the system and estimator variable definitions.

Smalarz, L., & Wells, G. (2024). Recommendations for the collection and preservation of eyewitness identification evidence. Applied Police Briefings, 1(1), 5-8. Read in full. A four-page practitioner summary of Wells and colleagues (2020) by two of that literature's authors, kept here as a second document carrying the 6,734 lineups and the one-in-four filler rate.

Wells, G. L., Small, M., Penrod, S., Malpass, R. S., Fulero, S. M., & Brimacombe, C. A. E. (1998). Eyewitness identification procedures: Recommendations for lineups and photospreads. Law and Human Behavior, 22(6), 603-647. Not read; metadata verified at Crossref and cited only as the review the 2020 paper updates.

National Research Council (2014). Identifying the Culprit: Assessing Eyewitness Identification. Washington: The National Academies Press. The summary chapter was read twice in the publisher's online reader. Source for the criticism of the Manson v. Brathwaite reliability test and for the recommendation to document witness confidence verbatim at the first identification.

Sporer, S. L., Penrod, S., Read, D., & Cutler, B. (1995). Choosing, confidence, and accuracy: A meta-analysis of the confidence-accuracy relation in eyewitness identification studies. Psychological Bulletin, 118(3), 315-327. Not read. Metadata verified at Crossref, which carries no abstract, and Semantic Scholar records the abstract as withheld by the publisher; PsycNet and ResearchGate answered with bot challenges on 21 September 2026. Its .41 for choosers is quoted here only through Wixted and Wells (2017), who are parties to the argument about what it means.

Sauerland, M., Tupper, N., Iannuzzi, M., & van Amelsvoort, A. (2023). The confidence-accuracy relationship for lineup decisions holds for the Dutch identification procedure. PLOS ONE, 18(4), e0284205. Read in full from the Europe PMC XML, fetched twice to identical text. Source for the 311 recruited and 293 analysed participants and for the correlations of .41 and .19.

Quigley-McBride, A., & Wells, G. L. (2023). Eyewitness confidence and decision time reflect identification accuracy in actual police lineups. Law and Human Behavior, 47(2), 333-347. Not read; closed at the publisher and blocked by a bot challenge at PsycNet on 21 September 2026. Its structured abstract was read at PubMed and is the only thing cited from it here.

Lindsay, D. S., & Mah, E. Y. (2021). Eyewitness identification can be studied in social contexts online with large samples in multi-lab collaborations. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition, 10(3), 328-334. Not read; metadata verified at Crossref, which carries no abstract. Cited only as what the search for multi-laboratory work on eyewitness identification returned, which is a case for such work rather than its result.
